Bash is ~41% of all tool use on this box. Not because the tools are missing — 690 of them
exist — but because nothing **routes** an agent from the shell command it was about to type
to the tool that already answers the question. The substitution registry is that routing
layer, and this doc is how to work on it.

Read this before you: add a row, promote a row, argue with a gate that blocked you, or ship
a new tool that is meant to replace a bash pattern.

## The one-paragraph model

A **pair** is `(bash pattern → tool)` plus a machine-checkable model of what the tool can
actually express. Pairs live in TypeScript. Each one is audited against real commands
sampled from real transcripts, which yields a **verdict**. The verdict caps the **tier** the
row may be enforced at. Everything an agent ever sees — the routing table in `CLAUDE.md`,
the advisory a PreToolUse hook attaches, the hard block on a policy violation — is a
*projection* of that same list, so prose and enforcement cannot drift apart.

## 1. The registry is the single source of truth

One list, three projections. Add a pair to the list and all three follow; edit a projection
by hand and a check fails the build.

```
packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/pairs/*.ts
                    │
                    ▼
              ALL_PAIRS  (pairs/index.ts)
                    │
    ┌───────────────┼────────────────────────────┐
    ▼               ▼                            ▼
equivalence.test  gen:tool-routing         seed:substitutions
 (the verdict)    → CLAUDE.md table    → harness_shared.bash_tool_substitutions
                       (what you read)     (what the PreToolUse gate enforces)
```

- **`ALL_PAIRS`** in `packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/pairs/index.ts` is the
  list. A pair not exported there is neither tested nor enforced; a pair added there is
  automatically both.
- It is **"pairs we have EVIDENCE about", not "pairs we enforce"** — negative results stay in
  the list on purpose. `PROCESS_PAIRS` carries a `not-a-substitute` verdict so the conclusion
  is durable and re-derived on every test run instead of being re-litigated every quarter.
  The routing generator filters those out of `CLAUDE.md`, and the database constraint pins
  them at `observe`.
- **The registry is DATA in Postgres, not logic in a hook** (D-002). The hooks contain no
  patterns; they ask the operator. That is why a row can be added, narrowed, or paused
  without touching a shell script.

### The three projections, and what guards each

| projection | written by | guarded by |
|---|---|---|
| the `CLAUDE.md` routing table | `npm run gen:tool-routing` | `npm run gen:tool-routing:check` — **fails the build** on drift (no DB needed) |
| the `bash_tool_substitutions` rows | `npm run seed:substitutions` | `npm run seed:substitutions:check` — **advisory**, exits 0 with a notice when PG is unreachable |
| the recorded verdict on each pair | the pair's `expectedVerdict` field | `equivalence.test.ts` recomputes it from the fixture and asserts equality |

`seed:substitutions:check` is deliberately advisory rather than a build gate: it needs
Postgres, and a check that reds the fleet gate every time PG is down gets deleted within a
week — a deleted check catches nothing. **Run it yourself after any edit under `pairs/`.**

> **Standing rule (D-020).** After ANY edit under
> `packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/pairs/`, run BOTH
> `npm run gen:tool-routing:check` and `npm run seed:substitutions:check`. A *new* pair or a
> *flipped verdict* additionally needs `npm run gen:tool-routing` (the WRITE) first, then a
> re-seed. Run them from the **repo root** — the shell's cwd leaks between calls and you will
> get `Missing script: seed:substitutions` from a subdirectory.
>
> D-020 exists because the ungated projection rotted while its gated sibling stayed correct:
> three separate changes updated `CLAUDE.md` (because `--check` fails the build) and updated
> the database not at all (because nothing checked and nothing ran). One row went on telling
> agents "there is no tool form for `ss`/`lsof`/`netstat`; keep using them" for days after
> `dev:listening_ports` shipped. **A seed script with no caller is not dormant, it is stale.**

## 2. Anatomy of a pair

Defined by `SubstitutionPair` in `packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/types.ts`:

| field | what it is |
|---|---|
| `id` | stable registry id, e.g. `file-read.sed-range` |
| `intentLabel` | the intent an advisory speaks about, e.g. `file-range-read`. **This is the registry KEY** (D-023) |
| `bashPattern` | a RegExp matched against ONE normalised atom |
| `toolName` | the tool that should have served it |
| `advisoryText` | the sentence the agent reads at `advise`/`deny` |
| `routing.{want,use,insteadOf}` | the three `CLAUDE.md` table cells — display fields, deliberately not derived |
| `expectedVerdict` | the verdict this pair is RECORDED as carrying — the anti-rot latch |
| `policyTier?` | the one authorized way to enter above `observe` (§5) |
| `holdAtObserve?` | the mirror: pin this row TO `observe`, whatever its verdict. Value is the required reason (§5) |
| `cover(atom)` | **the heart** — models what the tool can ACTUALLY express |

`cover()` is where the honesty lives. It must model the tool's real arguments and real
limits, read from the tool definition — not whether the tool is *nominally related* to the
command. A `cover()` that returns `{covered:true}` for everything produces an `equivalent`
verdict, which unlocks enforcement, which then blocks agents with no alternative. That is
the exact failure the equivalence gate exists to prevent (D-001).

When `cover()` says no, it must say **why**: `reason` is what makes a `needs-widening`
verdict actionable rather than a shrug.

### Pin the model to the real tool

A hand-written `cover()` is a *copy* of the tool's argument surface, and copies rot. Two
guards, both earned the hard way:

- **`expectedVerdict` catches pattern-side drift** — widen the pattern without re-recording
  the verdict and the test fails.
- It does **not** catch **tool-side** widening: the tool grows an argument, the model does
  not, and the pair silently under-claims forever. So a pair that hand-models its tool needs
  a **drift guard** tying the model to the real export (D-015), and that guard pins the
  tool's **argument surface**, not just the constants it copied (D-016). See
  `pairs/model-drift-helpers.ts` and `pairs/model-drift.test.ts`.

## 3. How to add a pair

### Step 0 — measure first, decide second

Every substantive decision in this registry was made by measurement, and several were made
*against* the intuition that preceded them. Before writing a pattern, get the population:
how many atoms, across how many distinct sessions, and what do the misses have in common?
The corpus helpers (`loadCorpusAtoms`, `sampleDistinct`, `buildFixture`) are in
`packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/corpus.ts`.

### Step 1 — write the pair

Add it to the right family file under `packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/pairs/`
(or a new one, exported from `pairs/index.ts`).

**Anchor the pattern on whole-command shape.** `atomize` splits on `|`, *including* a `|`
inside a quoted regex — so the search string of a `grep -E "npm install|npm ci"` becomes an
atom that looks exactly like a command (D-038). A `\b`-anchored pattern claims it and you
end up denying the mid-incident diagnostic. Patterns should also be **END-anchored** (D-023):
match the whole command shape, not a prefix of it.

### Step 2 — build the fixture from the pair's OWN pattern

The fixture is `fixtures/<pair-id>.sample.json`: `evidenceRef`, `extractedAt`, `totalAtoms`,
`totalSessions`, and a `sample[]` of `{sid, ts, atom}`. Build it by running **the pair's own
`bashPattern`** over the corpus — never by hand-picking commands you know the tool handles.
A hand-picked sample measures your imagination.

`fixtures/deps.unsafe-install.sample.json` and its builder are the template to copy.

### Step 3 — run the audit, read the verdict

```bash
npm run test:file -- packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/equivalence.test.ts
```

Record the computed verdict in `expectedVerdict`. If it is not what you expected, §4 says
which of the honest exits to take — **do not** widen `cover()` until it returns the verdict
you wanted.

### Step 4 — project it

```bash
npm run gen:tool-routing          # WRITE: regenerates the CLAUDE.md routing table
npm run gen:tool-routing:check    # must exit 0
npm run seed:substitutions        # upsert the rows (from the repo ROOT)
npm run seed:substitutions:check  # must exit 0
```

### Step 5 — **verify it LIVE** (§6). Not optional. This is the step that was missing.

## 4. The verdict and its three honest exits

`deriveVerdict` / `auditPair` in `equivalence.ts` produce one of:

| verdict | meaning | max tier |
|---|---|---|
| `equivalent` | every sampled command has a faithful tool expression | `advise` |
| `needs-widening` | some sampled commands have no tool expression — and it names them | `observe` |
| `not-a-substitute` | the tool answers a **different question**. Never gate this pattern | `observe` |
| `unaudited` | no audit has run | `observe` |

A `needs-widening` verdict has exactly **two** honest exits (D-008): **narrow the PATTERN**,
or **widen the TOOL**. Never lower the coverage bar. Which exit is right is decided by the
*shape of the misses*, not by taste — and in practice the misses cluster on a single axis
that tells you the answer. When every miss is a genuinely different question (socket STATE
vs socket LISTEN), the pattern was over-claiming: narrow it. When the misses are the
intent's *majority* case, the tool is not a substitute at all.

There is a third exit that is not a fix: record `not-a-substitute` and keep the row as a
durable negative result.

### The sample floor, and the census escape hatch

`MIN_SAMPLE_SIZE = 20` — but the sample is built with `sampleDistinct`, so it counts distinct
**spellings**, not commands. Read literally, the floor rejected any intent expressed in fewer
than 20 different ways: a statement about *vocabulary*, not evidence. It inverted its own
purpose — `^uptime`, 116 commands across 36 independent sessions, failed as "too rare to
enforce", while a 24-spelling pattern across 30 commands passed.

And low spelling-variety is precisely the property that makes a family worth acting on: an
intent everyone types **identically** is the one a single fixed answer can serve.

So `auditPair(pair, corpus, population?)` takes an optional population, and a pattern backed
by at least `MIN_POPULATION_ATOMS` atoms across `MIN_POPULATION_SESSIONS` (5) distinct
sessions clears the floor on **census** evidence instead of spelling variety (D-036). Use it
for homogeneous families; do not use it to rescue a pattern nobody actually runs.

## 5. The tier ladder: observe → advise → deny

Three tiers, reusing what the PreToolUse gate already implements. **Add no fourth
mechanism** (D-003).

- **`observe`** — a **staging** state. Emits nothing: both hooks act only on `advise`/`deny`,
  and `locks:check_command` returns the tier without recording it.
- **`advise`** — ride out as `additionalContext` on an **allow**. Teach, never block.
- **`deny`** — hard block. Reserved for rules that **already existed independently**.

### `observe` does not observe — `advise` is the observation window (D-042)

P-020 originally said: run at `observe` for 48h, then review hit-rate and false-positive
reports. That window could not work, and it is worth understanding why before you design
another one:

- **Nothing logs an `observe` match.** `pretooluse-bash-resource-gate.sh` acts only on
  `if _stier in ('advise','deny')`; `coord-hook.ts` is the same shape; `locks:check_command`
  computes the tier and records nothing.
- **Hit-rate never depended on the tier.** `bashAtoms` comes from `tool_usage_rollup`,
  attributed at session-ingest by replaying patterns over transcripts (native `Bash` never
  reaches `tool_invocations`, D-012). It accrues identically at any tier —
  `activity:bash-substitution-report` will tell you now.
- **False positives cannot arrive at `observe` at all.** A false-positive report needs an
  agent to SEE a claim and disagree. At `observe` nobody is shown anything, so
  `false_positive_count` is pinned at 0 by construction.

So the window could only ever conclude "48h elapsed, zero false positives" — the same
verdict whether the rules were perfect or catastrophic.

**`advise` is the real window.** It is the first visible tier, and it is safe to observe from
because it cannot block: the shell hook rides it out on an explicit `allow`, and OMP uses the
`followUp` reminder rather than `steer` (which aborts the in-flight tool). The full window and
the zero-false-positive bar still gate `advise → deny` — that is the transition P-020's
precedent is actually about (the shell-write guard false-positiving on a `>` inside a heredoc
**blocked** work).

**Don't wait for evidence you could go and measure.** Instead of a passive window, run the
documented caveats through the live registry and read the verdicts (§6). That is what
promoted these rows: 0/12 false positives across every caveat, `npm ci` still denied as the
positive control — and it caught a live defect two days of "observing" would never have
surfaced, because observing surfaces nothing.

> **A staging state that emits nothing is not an observation, and time spent in it is not
> evidence.** Before starting any clock, name the row that will be written while it runs. If
> nothing writes, the clock is a delay dressed as diligence.

### `equivalent` is not a mandate — a pair may hold itself back

A row can be provably equivalent and still be wrong to enforce: "the tool can express this"
and "the agent should be pushed to use it" are different claims. A pair states that with
**`holdAtObserve`**, whose value is the required reason:

```ts
holdAtObserve: 'D-011: capability:git is a pass-through, so this row offers the SAME answer…',
```

`promoteEarnedRows` skips a held row **and demotes one that has drifted above `observe`**.
That self-heal is not tidiness. D-011 recorded this hold for the git-read row in a decision
body — and a later promotion that selected on `equivalence_verdict` alone swept it into
`advise` anyway, firing the registry's largest advisory (~2,500 calls/week across 77 of 86
sessions) for a benefit D-011 had already argued was near-zero for the superuser role. The
seeder deliberately never demotes, so nothing would have pulled it back.

> **A constraint that lives only in prose will eventually be violated by someone acting in
> good faith on the data.** Carry it in the data — `holdAtObserve` is the mirror of
> `policyTier` (§5) for exactly this reason.

### The one authorized way past `observe`

`maxTierFor()` **never returns `deny`**. An equivalence score alone can never unlock a
block — no amount of measured coverage authorizes prohibition, because coverage is a *cost*
argument and a block is a *correctness* argument.

`deny` is a separate class: a rule that already existed independently of this registry, for
which the registry supplies a *mechanism* rather than a *judgement*. Such a rule has nothing
to observe — the decision was taken elsewhere, before the pattern was ever measured.

That authorization is carried **in the data**, not in reviewer memory (D-039):

```ts
// pairs/dependency-install.ts — the registry's only deny
intentLabel: 'policy-violation:unsafe-dependency-install',
policyTier: 'deny',
```

`assertPolicyTier()` refuses any pair that sets `policyTier` without the
`policy-violation:` prefix on its `intentLabel`, mirroring migration 665's
`tier_requires_equivalence` CHECK so the invariant is stated in the same terms on both sides
of the wire. A cost argument ("the tool is cheaper") can never reach `deny` this way.

**A deny's false-positive budget is ~0**, so its pattern must be *narrower than its problem*
(D-040) — and narrowed **structurally against the corpus**, not by imagination. The install
deny is the worked example: of 60 install-shaped atoms, 24 were `grep -E "npm install|npm ci"`
fragments (denying those blocks the mid-install diagnostic), and a named-package install may
target a scratch tree `install:safe` cannot reach. One readable rule covers both — the verb,
followed by nothing but flags and redirects.

## 6. Verify it LIVE — a green suite is not evidence the gate runs

**This is the most important section in this doc.** It is here because the registry spent its
entire first observation window enforcing *nothing*, behind 831 passing tests.

The failure (D-041, `EI-18787146155365536`): both PreToolUse hooks `JSON.parse` the result of
`locks:check_command`. The agent transport serializes a tabular result as **TOON**, not JSON.
The parse threw. The hooks are mandatorily **fail-open**, so the throw silently disabled
every resource hold *and* all 21 substitution rows — on both hook paths — and nothing logged
an error anywhere. The test suites never saw it because they stubbed the operator with JSON,
the one thing the real operator does not send.

Three generalisations, in increasing order of how much they will cost you:

1. **A fail-open client that never declares its wire format becomes a no-op the day the
   server starts compacting.** The fix is one line — `_meta: {'format': 'json'}` on the
   request — and the recurrence guard is a stub that *negotiates* rather than always
   replying JSON, so removing the declaration reds the tests.
2. **A stub that can only reply in one format can never observe a format bug.** If your test
   double is more cooperative than the real thing, it is not a test double.
3. **Seeding a row and reading a green suite is not shipping a rule.** Drive the real client
   against the running operator.

### The end-to-end check — run this for every row you add or promote

```bash
printf '%s' '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"npm ci"}}' \
  | PAPERCUSP_OPERATOR_URL=http://localhost:3170 \
    bash apps/operator/scripts/hooks/cc/pretooluse-bash-resource-gate.sh
```

Reading the result:

| output | meaning |
|---|---|
| a JSON `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision` | **the gate actually ran** — read the decision and the advisory text |
| **empty output** | **ALLOW** — which is also exactly what a total fail-open looks like |

That ambiguity is the whole trap: an empty response is indistinguishable from a dead client.
So **always run a positive control** — a command you expect the row to claim — and confirm it
produces a decision. Only then are your negative controls (the commands that must *not* be
claimed) meaningful.

Verified against `:3170` on 2026-07-27: `npm ci` → `deny` with the authored advisory;
`npm run install:safe` and `ls -la` → empty (allow).

Use `:3170` (staging), not `:3070`. The Hono host has no file-watch, and `:3070` serves the
green release checkout — your edit is not there yet. `dev:restart { target: 'staging',
confirm: true }` first if you changed server-side code.

## 7. Filing a false positive

If a row claimed a command it should not have — you were blocked, or advised, on something
the tool genuinely cannot express:

1. **File it.** `improvements:capture { kind: 'bug' }`, with the **raw command** verbatim,
   the row's `intentLabel`, and what the tool could not express. The raw command matters:
   classification is done on the raw string, and a paraphrase loses the shape that caused
   the match.
2. **The filing pauses that row's promotion.** It does not need anyone's agreement first.
3. **The fix is D-008's two exits** — narrow the pattern (usual) or widen the tool (when the
   miss is the intent's majority case). Never lower the coverage bar, and never special-case
   your one command.
4. **Do not route around a deny.** If the block is wrong, the pattern is wrong; fix the
   pattern. A deny's budget is ~0 false positives, so a real one is a genuine defect and is
   treated as such.

## 8. Definition of done for a NEW tool (D-004)

A tool that replaces a bash pattern is **DONE only with all three artifacts**:

1. **An equivalence-audit entry** proving it covers the real bash corpus it replaces —
   sampled from actual transcripts, not from imagination.
2. **A `bash_tool_substitutions` row**, so the gate advises on the bash form the moment the
   tool exists.
3. **A `CLAUDE.md` routing row**, generated from that same registry row.

The numbers behind this are unusually stark. 690 tools exist and Bash is still 41% of all
tool use. The one tool that had all three artifacts (`dev:pg_query`) sits at ~85% adoption;
the ones with none sit at ~1%. `install:safe` — a documented, mandated command with no
routing row — had **zero uses in seven days** while the unsafe form ran 60× across 15
sessions.

**A mandate with 0% adoption is a comment, not a mandate.** Shipping the tool is the easy
half; routing agents to it is the half that decides whether it exists in practice.

Two corollaries worth stating separately:

- **A mis-routing tool is fixed by making its description tell the truth** — not by widening
  it, and not by fighting the ranking (D-014).
- **A `not-a-substitute` row is never surfaced to an agent** (D-026). If the guidance you
  want to deliver is "do X instead of Y" for a pair that is *not* an equivalence, the
  registry is the wrong channel — that guidance belongs in `CLAUDE.md`.

## 9. Traps, in the order they will bite you

| trap | what happens | the rule |
|---|---|---|
| `\b`-anchored pattern | `atomize` splits inside quoted regexes, so a `grep -E "npm install\|npm ci"` search string becomes an atom that looks like a command; your row denies the diagnostic | anchor on whole-command shape, end-anchored (D-038, D-023) |
| hand-picked fixture | you measure your imagination, not the corpus | build the sample from the pair's OWN `bashPattern` |
| `cover()` returning true broadly | `equivalent` unlocks enforcement, then blocks agents with no alternative | model the tool's REAL argument surface (D-001) |
| editing `pairs/` and stopping at green tests | the DB rows silently rot; `CLAUDE.md` and the gate disagree | D-020: both `:check`s, from the repo root |
| running seeds from a subdirectory | `Missing script: seed:substitutions` — the shell's cwd leaks between calls | always `cd` to the repo root first |
| trusting a green suite | the client may not be talking to the server at all | §6 — drive the real hook against the running operator |
| probing `:3070` | it serves the green release checkout, not your edit | probe `:3170` after `dev:restart { target: 'staging' }` |
| promoting on `equivalent` alone | equivalence is a capability claim, not a mandate (D-011) | promotion needs the observation window too |

## Where the numbers come from

The substitution metric is counted **at ingest from transcripts**, never from Postgres
(D-012), and the intent **bucket is matched at ingest**, not derived from a verb at read time
(D-013) — see `packages/operator-core/lib/search/session-ingest.ts` and
`packages/operator-core/lib/bash-substitution/usage-rollup.ts`.

Measure **per-bucket, not in aggregate** (D-006). A bucket that does not move after its row
lands is a signal, and it says which of two things went wrong: the tool is not actually
equivalent (send it back to the equivalence audit), or the advisory text is not landing
(rewrite it). Record which, per bucket. Do not declare success on the aggregate number.
